title: Sound
standard_text: Sound waves are longitudinal waves made of compressions and rarefactions; the speed of sound in different media; pitch and frequency, loudness and amplitude; echoes; ultrasound and its uses. (summary of the senior secondary Physics curriculum, SSS 2; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 2 Physics worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): sound and echoes, sound in air, sound, resonance and standing waves, ultrasound and technology and pitch, loudness and speed. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Pitch depends on frequency; loudness on amplitude.
key_sub: Sound needs a medium; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
body_html:
How to think about it

Sound is a longitudinal wave: a vibrating object makes compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread out). Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases; in air it travels at about 340 m·s⁻¹.

A higher frequency gives a higher pitch; a larger amplitude gives a louder sound. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; ultrasound is above 20,000 Hz and is used for scans of unborn babies and to find distances by echoes.

Example

An echo returns after 2 s. The speed of sound is 340 m·s⁻¹. How far is the wall?

The sound goes there and back.

Answer: 340 m

Example

Which has a higher pitch, 500 Hz or 1,000 Hz?

Pitch depends on frequency.

Answer: 1,000 Hz

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to halve the distance for an echo.
  • Thinking sound travels fastest in air.
  • Mixing up pitch and loudness.

faq.q: Why can astronauts not hear each other in space without radios?
faq.a: Space is a vacuum and sound needs a medium.
They send pulses down and time the echoes to measure the depth of the sea (sonar).

items.q: What kind of wave is sound in air?
items.e: Air particles move along the direction of the wave.

items.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest: air, water, steel or a vacuum?
items.e: Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, and cannot travel in a vacuum.
